article_text:
If Gen Z is out shopping, then Frieze London should be its natural habitat, right? Fifteen dealers in the tent beg to differ

This is excerpted from Monopol International's new weekly English newsletter. Sign up here to read it.

VIPs went art-hunting at Frieze Art Fair and I went looking for people under 30 who buy art. As it turns out, they’re an elusive bunch, which is not what you’d expect given the headlines generated by Clare McAndrew ’s Art Basel and UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026, released last week. According to a survey of 3,100 collectors, Gen Z makes up the biggest spending demographic in the art market. It was a deus ex machina for the art world, which has been hungrily hunting for a new horizon for years, eager to future-proof itself. First it was the promise of an exploding Asian market, then of digital art and NFTs, and of the Middle East. Now, Gen Z have been tasked with its rebooting.

But—as my high school economics teacher told us—statistics are more of an art than a science. Data is malleable; you can make it do what you want within reason. The yearning to render something as wide as the art world empirical is one-part helpful, two-parts silly. (“Multiple realities can exist within the same minute at the same fair one booth over,” as one dealer told me at Frieze .) Any reports about “mood” are brave but fallible captures of what 300-plus businesses may be experiencing on a sunny Wednesday in a big white tent in London.

You’ve already read all about it : In 2025, Gen Z (those born between 1997 and 2012) spent nearly three times the survey-wide average of $124,265 by older generations. The report concedes that its sample size is specific and small: 279 of the 3,100 respondents were themselves Gen Z. Around 15 of them made up nearly half of the roughly 31 respondents who bought a work priced above $1 million in 2025 and the first half of 2026.

The report fueled chatter (and hopes and dreams) at Frieze this past week, and ahead of Art Basel Paris next week. At Niru Ratnam in Fitzrovia, Tim Schneider , Georgina Adam , and Ratnam hosted a talk about next-generation collectors: “This demographic has less willingness to debase themselves to be able to purchase paintings,” said Schneider, while also pouring cold water on the hope that this generation (who, I should add, are still largely aged 17–25) is going to do what their elders did with the whack of cash dropped on them from the so-called Great Wealth Transfer. “The belief among a certain faction of the market that this money will cleanly transfer down, and that they’ll buy art with it,” continued Schneider, “is a bit far-fetched.” A few 20-something visitors trickled in late to the talk and took notes. One of them, sitting a row in front of me, giggled when the topic of Gen Z screen time habits came up.

On to Frieze. According to McAndrew , 73% of her Gen Z cohort make purchases at art fairs, second only to spendy boomers, at 77%. By that logic, Frieze is exactly where they should be visible, right? My quest was about as anecdotal as it gets, but I wanted to see what gallerists were experiencing. The verdict from the 15 I talked to: Gen Z isn’t really there. Not one dealer told me they witnessed a significant new buyer generation emerging. And they’re worried.

The replies were pretty stark. “Bullshit,” said one dealer in the Focus section, the part of the fair for emerging artists. “The profession is aging so quickly,” he added, noting that the vast majority of his collector base is now 50 and up. Four dealers told me that interfamilial collecting is quite a thing—but it makes it hard to say who’s spending, and where the work is hanging. A daughter may pick out a work, but mom may pay for it. So, who is the collector?

“You’re excited when you have one or two Gen Z buyers,” said one Austrian dealer. “And if they exist, they’re in Asia,” another echoed.

We Millennials, now roughly 30–45 years old, can remember a flush and fun, low-interest-rate art market. That’s when the bulk of us entered the work force in this industry. Younger professionals are working under no delusions now, having likely missed much of that era, and having started their careers in a pandemic-leveled, locked down, high-interest-rate economy.

“What’s stated in the report is the opposite of what’s actually been happening,” said one dealer. “If anything is true from that survey, it’s that Gen Z collectors follow their parents in terms of taste, in terms of historically valuable art, but I don’t see room for experimentation and trust anymore. It takes twice as long to get support for young artists. What’s being sold are the sure bets based on Sotheby’s and Christie’s . The galleries have lost the confidence of collectors by pumping a system that didn’t work out. Young collectors don’t trust this system. They’re much more careful with their money.”

So, Gen Z: not yet officially trending—at least not along the aisles I wandered down. But, age is nothing but a number, and as we in the art business know well, numbers can be fudged.

article_text:
Bringing together more than 80 artists and authors, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes’ examines how colonial histories constructed the boundaries between civilisation and barbarism, and how those categories continue to shape bodies, territories and knowledge.

At TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes ’ brings historical material into conversation with contemporary art to reconsider the systems that have classified cultures and people. Spanning artworks, films, photographs, documents, and objects, the exhibition connects the Canary Islands with Africa, Europe, the Caribbean, and Latin America through histories of colonial expansion, migration, and exchange.

Curated by Alejandro Castañeda, Néstor Delgado, Katya García-Antón, Roberto Gil, Narelys Hernández, Joel Peláez and Sergio Rubira, the exhibition features more than 80 artists and authors, including Sammy Baloji, Yto Barrada, Ana Mendieta, Wifredo Lam, Abdoulaye Konaté, Coco Fusco and Carlos Motta.

Across five interconnected sections, ‘Mientras seamos salvajes’ explores representations of Indigenous peoples, the divide between the so-called “wild” and “civilised”, alternative systems of knowledge, labour and extractivism, and the museum’s role in producing historical narratives. Rather than simply dismantling inherited categories, the exhibition asks what other relationships, forms of knowledge and futures might emerge beyond them.

This exhibition is on view at TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes in Santa Cruz until 24 January 2027.

"第二次世界大战之后的1950年代，是日本版画国际评价不断提高的时代。在1951（昭和26）年的圣保罗双年展上与斋藤清一同获得“圣保罗日本人奖”的驹井哲郎（1920～1976）便是这一时期崭露头角的作家之一。在1940年代后期作为版画家正式开始活动的驹井，在56岁骤然离世之前发表了大量作品，同时在多摩美术大学和东京艺术大学执教，为日本铜版画的普及和地位提升做出了贡献。本次展览正值其逝世50周年之际举办，以驹井作品收藏家、原资生堂名誉会长福原义春捐赠给世田谷美术馆的“福原义春收藏”为核心，追溯驹井的艺术生涯。", "paragraph", "text": "展览由〈第1章 觉醒于版画［1920-1948］〉〈第2章 渐趋充盈的梦与抒情［1948-1955］〉〈第3章 黑与白的深渊［1956-1976］〉〈第4章 美丽的色彩世界［1956-1976］〉〈第5章 憧憬与探求——敬爱的作家们与其心爱之物〉这５个章节构成。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "出生于东京日本桥的驹井，在就读庆应义塾普通部15岁时邂逅了铜版画，并前往位于东京麹町、由西田武雄主导的日本蚀刻研究所学习，接受了基础技法的指导。战时毕业于东京美术学校的驹井于1947（昭和22）年加入恩地孝四郎主导的“一木会”同人，与创作版画系的版画家们频繁交流，等待着飞跃的契机。这就是〈第1章〉中所介绍的年轻时期的驹井的面貌。", "translated": true}, "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "探索“黑与白”的驹井，其实色彩感觉也极为丰富。这些能够让人感受到保罗·克利等人影响的作品，往往流露出幽默感与童心。展厅现场左侧绘有蜗牛的版本是与安东次男合作的第2部诗画集《人称其为反歌》。由于驹井遭遇交通事故身受重伤，从1962年构思到完成历时4年，但据说两人是在坦率讨论的基础上共同创作的。", "汇集与驹井渊源深厚的国内外作家以及驹井心爱之物的，是〈第5章〉。以打磨黑白表现而闻名的版画家是长谷川洁，如前所述，驹井非常敬爱长谷川。话虽如此，若将此处展示的作品进行对比，笔者不禁觉得在“黑与白”的意趣上，与驹井更接近的或许是法国版画家奥迪隆·雷东。这纯属“个人感想”。雷东也是驹井所敬爱的作家之一，其作品同样在本次展览中展出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展出的不仅是这些作品。据说在驹井的工作室里，除了心爱的工具之外，还留下了许多铜质和锌质的原版，这些物品也能在此大量看到。在接触这些物品的过程中，驹井哲郎这位人物的真实面貌也渐渐浮现出来。从作品到相关资料，可以从各个角度俯瞰驹井的人生。可以说这是一个无愧于纪念年份的展览。（美术展导航 田中聪）", "translated": true}, {"type": article_text:
銅版画家・駒井哲郎 掌上にひろがる星座のように

会場：神奈川県立近代美術館 葉山（神奈川県三浦郡葉山町一色２２０８－１）

会期：２０２６年９月１２日（土）～１１月１５日（日）

休館日：月曜休館、ただし９月２１日、１０月１２日は開館

開館時間：９：３０～１７：００（入館は閉館の３０分前まで）

アクセス：JR横須賀線「逗子」駅前の「東口3番のりば」から京浜急行バス「逗11、12系統（海岸回り）」に乗車し、「三ヶ丘・神奈川県立近代美術館前」で下車（所要時間約20分)、京浜急行「逗子・葉山」駅前の「南口2番のりば」から京浜急行バス「逗11、12系統（海岸回り）」に乗車し、「三ヶ丘・神奈川県立近代美術館前」で下車（所要時間約18分)

観覧料：一般１２００円、２０歳未満・学生１０５０円、６５歳以上６００円、高校生１００円、中学生以下と障害者手帳などミライロIDを提示の方（および介助者原則１名）は無料

※１０月１１日（葉山館開館記念日）と１１月３日（文化の日）は無料開館日 ※詳細情報は ホームページ で確認を

第二次世界大戦の後、1950年代は、日本の版画が国際的な評価を高めた時代だった。1951（昭和26）年のサンパウロ・ビエンナーレで斎藤清とともに「在聖日本人賞」を受賞した駒井哲郎（1920～1976）はこの時代に頭角を現した作家のひとりである。1940年代後半に版画家として本格的な活動を始めた駒井は、56歳で急逝するまで多くの作品を発表するとともに、多摩美術大学や東京藝術大学で教鞭を執り、日本での銅版画の普及・地位向上に貢献した。没後50年を機に開かれるこの展覧会は、駒井作品のコレクターだった元資生堂名誉会長・福原義春氏が世田谷美術館に寄贈した「福原義春コレクション」を中心に、駒井の画業をたどる回顧展である。

展覧会は〈第１章 版画へのめざめ［1920-1948］〉〈第２章 満ちてゆく夢と抒情［1948-1955］〉〈第３章 白と黒の深淵［1956-1976］〉〈第４章 美しき色彩の世界［1956-1976］〉〈第５章 憧憬と探求―敬愛した作家たちと、愛用品〉の５章で構成されている。

東京・日本橋で生まれた駒井は、慶應義塾普通部に通っていた15歳の頃に銅版画と出会い、東京・麹町にあった西田武雄主宰の日本エッチング研究所に通って、基本的な技法の手ほどきを受けたという。戦時中に東京美術学校を卒業した駒井は1947（昭和22）年、恩地孝四郎の主宰する「一木会」の同人となり、創作版画系の版画家たちとの交流を重ね、飛躍の時を待つ。というのが、〈第１章〉で紹介される若き日の駒井の姿である。

続く〈第２章〉では、内外で賞を獲得し、版画家として知られるようになった駒井が、試行錯誤を重ねながら独自の作風を築き上げていく時期の作品を集めた。冒頭に挙げた《束の間の幻影》は、前述したサンパウロ・ビエンナーレでの「在聖日本人賞」受賞作品。下の《孤独な鳥》は、それに先立つ1947年、「春陽会第27回展」で春陽会賞を受賞した作品だ。この作品を含め、この時期、駒井はレースや葉の模様を転写した作品を複数制作しているのだが、この手法には駒井が敬愛する長谷川潔や恩地の影響がうかがえるという。さらに駒井は1952年、若手の芸術家たちが集う「実験工房」に評論家・瀧口修造の推薦で参加。まさに順風満帆なキャリアである。1954年には、フランス政府私費留学生試験に合格し、パリで版画を学ぶことになるのだが、ここでは本場の作品の質の高さに圧倒され、自信を喪失してしまったともいう。

帰国後、自分の作品を見直し、新たな境地を拓いていく駒井。「銅版画の良さはやっぱり黒の世界にあると思う」と語り、「白と黒による表現を銅版画の真髄」と考えていた駒井の、モノクロームの作品を集めたのが〈第３章〉である。詩人・安東次男と共作した詩画集『からんどりえ（CALENDRIER）』、銅版画集『九つの夢から』などで展開される白と黒のコントラスト。それについて駒井は「すべての色彩の極限、もっとも単純で、もっとも複雑な色彩」と述べている。ちなみに『九つの夢から』は埴谷雄高の連作『闇のなかの黒い馬』の挿絵をベースにして制作されたものである。

「白と黒」を探求した駒井だが、実は色彩感覚も豊か。パウル・クレーらの影響の感じられるそれらの作品は、ユーモラスで遊び心を感じさせることも多いという。展示風景の左側、カタツムリが描かれている版本は、安東次男と組んだ２作目の詩画集『人それを呼んで反歌という』。駒井が交通事故で大けがを負ったため、1962年の構想から完成まで４年を要したが、ふたりで率直な議論を交わしながら制作したのだそうだ。

その駒井と縁の深い内外の作家や、駒井の愛用品を集めたのが〈第５章〉。白と黒の表現を磨き上げた版画家として有名なのが長谷川潔で、前述の通り、駒井は長谷川を敬愛していた。とはいえ、ここで展示されている作品を見比べると、「白と黒」のニュアンスで駒井に近いのは、フランスの版画家、オディロン・ルドンなのではないだろうか、とも思う。あくまで「個人の感想」だが。ルドンは駒井が敬愛する作家のひとりであり、その作品もやはりここで展示されている。

展示されているのは、それら作品だけではない。駒井のアトリエには、愛用の道具と鞆に銅や亜鉛の原版も多数残されていたそうで、それらの品物も数多く見ることができる。それらに触れているうちに、何となく駒井哲郎という人物の素顔も見えてくるのである。作品、関連資料を含め、様々な角度から駒井の人生が鳥瞰できる。メモリアルイヤーにふさわしい展覧会といえるだろう。（美術展ナビ 田中聡）

On Saturday, at a gun range, a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury to film director Michael Mann . He was treated and is being released.

Mann is scheduled to direct Heat 2 in January. Deadline spoke exclusively to a source close to the filmmaker, and this will not impact start of production on that sequel to the classic crime thriller, Deadline understands. More to come…

article_text:
To shoot their Oscar-contending film Still Standing , directors Víctor Tadashi Suárez and Livia Albeck-Ripka donned hazmat suits – for good reason.

Their documentary, winner of Oscar-qualifying awards at Full Frame, the Seattle International Film Festival, and Aspen Shortsfest, explores homes left toxic by the catastrophic Eaton fire that tore through the Altadena section of Los Angeles in January 2025. That wildfire destroyed thousands of homes in Altadena alone, but owners of homes that survived – the houses still standing – faced an impossible dilemma: should they risk their health to return home?

Related Stories

Doc Talk Podcast: 'Remake' Director Ross McElwee On Love, Loss And Grieving For His Son

Spencer Pratt To The Rescue? Failed L.A. Mayoral Candidate Wants To Help Trump Save Hollywood, Supposedly

“To enter toxic homes, we wore hazmat suits and masks, and covered our car in plastic sheeting,” the directors write. “This is the second time that we have made a film together about wildfires. We met in January 2020, working on a film about the Australian bushfires for The New York Times Presents.”

Watch on Deadline

Still Standing screened at SFFILM’s Doc Stories in San Francisco this weekend. It screens at the San Diego Asian Film Festival Sunday, at UnionDocs in Queens, New York on Monday, and at Cameraimage in Torún, Poland on Friday, among other festivals this month. The film screened at the Bend Film Festival in Oregon last month, where it won Best Documentary Short. The documentary won Best Cinematography at the Nevada City Film Festival, selected from among all genres in competition.

“After the Los Angeles wildfires, thousands of homes remain standing, yet contaminated with toxic ash. Many insurers tell residents their homes are habitable,” reads a synopsis. Moving back in under such circumstances presents a wrenching choice. “Shot from the inside of toxic homes on 16mm film, Still Standing considers what it means to survive one disaster only to face another.”

Tadashi Suárez and Livia Albeck-Ripka are a filmmaking couple based in LA.

“We live in Los Angeles, about 10 miles from one of the neighborhoods that burned in last year’s wildfires,” they write in their directors’ statement. “In the months that followed, the city began to return to normal, and those who lost homes began rebuilding. But there was another, quieter, and in some ways more horrifying reality unfolding for those whose homes were still standing.”

The directors’ statement continues, “We first learned of this situation through our close friend, Roy Werner, who also composed the score for this film. He, his wife and infant daughter had been unable to return home for months. Their house was the first we filmed in. At that time, there was barely any published reporting about the toxicity of standing homes.

“Over the next six months, we interviewed more than two dozen residents, researchers, and environmental consultants, and filmed in more than a dozen homes. They were time capsules frozen from the moment before the disaster, with Christmas decorations still up and tables set for family gatherings; like scenes from Pompeii or Chernobyl. Residents were caught in a liminal space where loss and grief are undefined. They spent their days on an endless cycles of phone calls to insurance companies and adjusters.”

Still Standing is executive produced by Kevin Iwashina (former head of documentary at Fifth Season and former president of the IDA board of directors), and three-time Emmy-nominated filmmaker Bernardo Ruiz.

Still Standing premieres online on November 19 as as part of the 9 th season of the PBS series POV .

article_text:
全国の美術館や博物館などのグッズが一堂に会するイベント「美術展ナビフェス2026」を9月29日、東京・大手町のよみうり大手町小ホールで開催しました。

全ブース紹介は今回が最終回となりました。

会場に潜入！「美術展ナビフェス2026」の全ブースを大公開（その１）新規出展館のブースをめぐる▶

会場に潜入！「美術展ナビフェス2026」の全ブースを大公開（その２）会場で見つけた個性豊かなグッズを紹介▶

会場に潜入！「美術展ナビフェス2026」の全ブースを大公開（その３）モネ、北斎、トラりん、ぷっくりシール！人気のグッズが目白押し▶

まだまだ魅力的なブースがたくさんありますよ！さっそくブースをのぞいてみましょう。（※商品はタイミングにより品切れの場合がございます）

大阪中之島美術館

おしゃれで洗練されたグッズが印象的な大阪中之島美術館のブースにやってきました。中央にある「Azuma Bukuro」は シンプルでありながら、タフで機能的 。美術展ナビフェスでも毎年多くの方が手に取る人気商品です。

同館を代表する収蔵品、佐伯祐三「郵便配達夫」をモチーフにしたマグネットも見逃せません。ルネ・マグリット「レディ・メイドの花束」のモチーフも新たに登場しました。美術館とグッズショップのインスタグラムのアカウントをフォローすると、好きなポストカードを2枚いただけました！うれしい！

大阪中之島美術館 のグッズはこちら▶

丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館

丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館のブースにやってきました。香川県丸亀市ゆかりの画家・猪熊弦一郎の作品をモチーフにしたミュージアムグッズがたくさん並んでいます。

猪熊弦一郎と言えば、JR上野駅中央改札の壁画《自由》を見たことがある方も多いのではないでしょうか。壁画《自由》をモチーフにした缶バッジや、原画がプリントされたマスキングテープや一筆箋などが新登場。

定番商品「猪熊猪口」は丸亀らしくうどん猪口として使うもよし、鉢カバーなどインテリアに使ってもおしゃれです。

丸亀市猪熊弦一郎現代美術館 のグッズはこちら▶

慶應義塾ミュージアム・コモンズ

体験型のブースで会場を盛り上げていたのは、慶應義塾ミュージアム・コモンズの学生さんたち。今年は6月から7月にかけて開催された「『ガリヴァー旅行記』300年 ガリヴァーと奇想天外！ワンダーランド」展 に ちなみ「AIガリヴァー」というプログラムを楽しみました。

注目のグッズは額入りの「木馬に乗るガリヴァーの刺繍」です。 購入者限定で刺繍データを配布されるそうで、刺繍ミシンを使えば自身でさまざまなガリヴァーグッズを作ることができます。

慶應義塾ミュージアム・コモンズのグッズはこちら▶

五島美術館

五島美術館のブースにやってきました。 裏面いっぱいに作品の絵柄があしらわれた 一筆箋は、美術館のグッズショップでも売れ筋のアイテムです。

同館を代表する作品のひとつ「重要文化財 古伊賀水指 銘 破袋」を大胆にプリントしたトートバッグが目をひきました。毎年リピーターも多い人気のカレンダーにも注目です。

五島美術館 のグッズはこちら▶

出光美術館

出光美術館のブースにやってきました。出光美術館の「仙厓カレンダー」も毎年リピーターの多い人気のカレンダーです。この「仙厓カレンダー」、なんと 70年以上にわたって発行されているそう。

おすすめ商品は、「絵はがきセット〈福 F U K U〉」です。 仙厓の「鯛釣恵比寿画賛」や尾形乾山の「銹絵染付金銀白彩松波文蓋物」など、 同館が所蔵するおめでたいモチーフ作品がいっぱいです。

出光美術館のグッズはこちら▶

article_text:
The National Park Service has revised its plans to redevelop the Tidal Basin region of the National Mall in Washington, DC. The plan zeroes in on West Potomac Park, which Trump picked in May as his preferred site for the planned National Garden of American Heroes . One leading historic preservationist interpreted the plan as a way to create space for the project, reports the Washington Post .

“The plan that we saw is really about making the space for the Garden of Heroes,” Charles A. Birnbaum, founding president and CEO of the nonprofit Cultural Landscape Foundation, told the paper, adding that, however, “the Garden of Heroes is not included in the plan” and that it “feels like a placeholder for something else that’s going to be inserted.” The Cultural Landscape Foundation, headquartered in DC, was established in 1998 to educate the public about the nation’s shared landscape heritage. It calls attention to threatened sites and gives a biennial $100,000 landscape architecture prize.

The development plan, according to a document published by NPS , is meant to address issues including compacted soil, exposed tree roots, flooding of sidewalks, and damage to the area’s famed cherry trees. An updated concept for the northwest zone of the area is dominated by multi-use fields and an oval lawn; the initial plan included more features, such as a softball field, a bike path, a parking area, and a comfort station.

Birnbaum isn’t the only one whose suspicions were raised by the plan.

“Ovals are not actually that great for athletic fields,” Thomas Luebke, the secretary of the Commission of Fine Arts, said during the meeting . “I think it strikes everybody here that there’s something else going on.”

The proposed sculpture park was conceived by Trump and would see a wide-range of historical figures displayed alongside one another, including George Washington, Alex Trebek, the longtime host of TV game show Jeopardy! , and Harriet Tubman. Sculpted in traditional materials at larger than life size, these sculptures have been on his mind for six years, and he has publicly promised “a beautiful complex.”

Six preservationist organizations sued in June to stop the project, saying it could not proceed without congressional approval. In April, CNN had reported that not one sculpture would likely be standing by the targeted July 4, 2026, opening date, a projection ultimately proven true.
excerpt_original: A key conservationist called the plan a game of “three-card monte.”

article_text:
Cine

Sensatez y sentimiento – Crítica de la película

Gerardo Frías

Aunque no reinventa el texto de Jane Austen, destaca por su diseño de producción y fotografía.

Cada cierto tiempo, Hollywood vuelve a Jane Austen, y Sensatez y sentimiento no es la excepción: llega menos de un año después de que se cumplieran 250 años del nacimiento de la autora, y de la mano de Working Title, la casa que ya se ha movido con soltura por este universo. La pregunta inevitable es por qué volver a contar una historia que el cine ya nos contó de forma tan memorable en 1995, con la dirección de Ang Lee, un guion ganador del Óscar escrito por Emma Thompson y un reparto encabezado por la propia Thompson, Kate Winslet y Hugh Grant. Esta nueva versión, dirigida por Georgia Oakley, responde con un refrito que se acerca un poco más a nuestra época, y lo hace con un reparto principal menos mainstream que aquel, algo que, curiosamente, le sienta bien.

La historia es sencilla: los pesares amorosos de dos hermanas, Elinor (Daisy Edgar-Jones) y Marianne (Esmé Creed-Miles), cuya familia queda en una situación económica precaria tras la muerte del padre. Como en cualquier película de época de este estilo, todo gira en torno a la pertenencia y a la necesidad monetaria de la mujer frente al hombre, una temática común en las historias que dramatizan la Inglaterra georgiana. Por eso es cierto que el drama romántico se siente sencillo, incluso repetitivo. Pero la realidad es que no aburre: repetitivo o no, te mantiene al tanto de si nuestras protagonistas volverán a cometer un error o si ahora sí avanzará la trama.

Su mayor fuerza, y muy en línea con el género, está en el diseño de arte y la fotografía. Escenarios y vestuarios están perfectamente realizados y acompañados por una fotografía naturalista que da vida a todos los colores de la película, con una atmósfera mucho más gris y melancólica tanto en el viejo Londres como en la playa a la que se mudan las protagonistas, y cargada de calidez y armonía cada vez que las hermanas mejoran su lazo. La música, por su parte, nos entrega el estado emocional de cada escena sin apegarse demasiado a una música de época: en ningún punto se siente exagerada, y junto con la fotografía acompaña a la perfección el contexto histórico, emocional y situacional de la cinta.

Mi reserva está en el corazón que la película dice tener. En cierto punto plantea que lo importante no son las relaciones amorosas que ambas forman a lo largo de la cinta, sino su lazo como hermanas y como familia. La intención se nota, y de a kilómetros se distingue cuál de nuestras protagonistas es Sensatez y cuál es Sentimiento, ademas de dejarnos ver el que ambas deberían ser un poco mas como la otra, pero creo que esta parte se queda corta: faltó explorar mucho más su relación, porque la mayor parte del tiempo las vemos juntas, pero separadas, cada una en su mundo.

Lo que sí hay que aplaudir a más no poder, y lo que se lleva la película, es Fiona Shaw como la señora Jennings. Te hace reír, te hace sentir incómodo, te hace reír de nuevo, y funciona hasta cierto punto como el hilo conductor de las decisiones más acertadas de nuestras protagonistas. Es sin duda el personaje más carismático de la cinta y, en lo relativamente poco que la vemos nos muestra un trabajo de dirección, de casting y de actuación simplemente maravilloso.

Con todo, esta es una versión que cumple: no reinventa a Austen ni supera a la de 1995, pero luce preciosa, suena bien y tiene en la señora Jennings una razón de sobra para ir a verla.

Gerardo Frías

article_text:
Director Zach Cregger ‘s “ Resident Evil ” has notched a notable box office milestone, climbing to $400 million in global ticket sales.

His reboot of the ’90s zombie video game has earned $157.399 million in North America and $242.6 million overseas for a worldwide haul of exactly $400 million. It’s now the highest-grossing installment in the 24-year-old horror franchise, toppling 2016’s “Resident Evil: The Final Chapter” with $312 million globally. And it ranks as Cregger’s biggest film to date, ranking above 2022’s low-budget success “Barbarian” with $46 million and 2025’s sleeper hit “Weapons” with a mighty $270 million worldwide.

Related Stories

Harry Styles Waltzes His Way Through 'Coming Up Roses' Music Video

Harry Styles Debuts Unreleased Song He Wrote in Memory of Liam Payne, 'What Is Enough,' on Second Anniversary of Ex-Bandmate's Death

“Resident Evil” opened in September to a series-best $60 million domestically and $108 million globally. That distinction previously belonged to 2010’s “Resident Evil: Afterlife” with $26 million, not adjusted for inflation. Buoyed by great reviews and positive audience scores, the movie remained a draw throughout October, a prime time for scary movies. Top overseas markets include China with $71.4 million, the United Kingdom with $19.4 million and Mexico with $12.7 million.

Cregger’s take on the material — “Weapons” actor Austin Abrams plays a medical courier who fights through a viral outbreak of infested monsters in Raccoon City — comes five years after the studio last attempted to revive the property. That effort, 2021’s “Resident Evil: Welcome to Raccoon City,” was a critical and commercial failure with $42 million worldwide against a $25 million budget. The Capcom video game was first adapted for the big screen in 2002’s “Resident Evil,” starring Milla Jovovich. She reprised her role as Alice, a former security specialist and covert operative, in five follow-up films in the 2000s and 2010s.

Sony produced this version of “Resident Evil” for $75 million, so the sci-fi horror film will turn a tidy profit for the studio. Sony followed up this win, and the summer’s sensation “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” (the third-biggest movie ever with $2.5 billion) with back-to-back duds. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning” left theaters with a paltry $9 million in North America and $17 million globally against a $30 million budget, while Taika Waititi’s literary adaptation “Klara and Sun” has barely cracked $1 million domestically against a $20 million budget.

title_original: Tesfaye Urgessa 特斯法耶・烏爾蓋薩
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "In the sterile, white-walled space of White Cube Hong Kong, Tesfaye Urgessa’s new paintings seem to radiate a contained intensity. Clusters of figures emerge from layered surfaces at once frozen and in motion, inhabiting interiors and chaotic tableaux. Across the canvas, rough, raw marks sit in deliberate tension with passages of refined detail. The exhibition, The Lingering Departure , marks Urgessa’s first show with the gallery since joining in August. It follows his first solo museum presentation in Asia, at the Red Brick Art Museum in Beijing, and brings together works created over the past year in Addis Ababa and Stuttgart."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Taken from one of the paintings’ titles, The Lingering Departure captures the emotional core of Urgessa’s practice, the idea that leaving is never reduced to a single moment but is a state that begins before departure and continues long after arrival. “A departure sounds sudden, while lingering suggests something that remains,” emails Urgessa from his studio in Germany. “Before any physical or psychological change happens, there is a period of anticipation. Then the departure takes place but the place you left does not disappear. It stays with you through memory.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A biographical arc of childhood and art training in Ethiopia, migration to Germany and now a practice that moves between continents gives weight to the artist’s assertion that the place you left does not disappear. Born in Addis Ababa in 1983, Urgessa grew up in a family where art was woven into the quotidian, watching his father draw portraits from photographs of neighbours. “I think seeing him draw and paint created an interest in me to start drawing myself when I was very young,” he says. “But I didn’t really know, until quite late in my teenage years, that there was a whole world of art or that becoming an artist could actually be a profession.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "His early visual education came not from galleries or textbooks but from copying the flat, vivid figures of Ethiopian Orthodox church murals, an experience that embedded a distinct way of seeing into his work. “The frontal gaze of the figures, the vivid and bright colours but also the simplicity and flatness of the compositions – those qualities stayed with me visually,” he explains."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tesfaye-Urgessa-The-Lingering-Departure-White-Cube-Hong-Kong-9-September-%E2%80%93-20-October-2026_1-copy-2.jpeg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Installation view of Tesfaye Urgessa The Lingering Departure at White Cube Hong Kong, 9 September – 20 October 2026. © Tesfaye Urgessa. Photo: © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was only later, at art school in Ethiopia and then in Germany, where he enrolled at the State Academy of Fine Arts Stuttgart in 2009, that he encountered a wider art history, sharpening the questions of identity that had previously remained unspoken and would become foundational to his practice. “I don’t really remember thinking about my identity in the same way before I came to Germany,” he admits. “Being in a different country and culture made me much more aware of where I came from and how I was perceived by others.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The physical departure from Addis Ababa did not erase Ethiopia; instead, it became a psychological presence that travelled with him, refracted through memory, language and the politics of belonging in Europe. As migration grew, these questions grew louder in his work. “It made me think more deeply about migration, belonging, exclusion and the way societies decide who belongs and who does not,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yet the paintings avoid falling into didacticism: they are not illustrations of political arguments but spaces in which psychological and social tensions coexist. Urgessa’s figures, often suspended in kinetic, dense compositions where objects and figures coexist alongside one another, seem to embody this condition of being neither fully rooted nor entirely adrift, existing in a liminal space shaped by displacement. It was fitting, then, that he was the first artist to represent Ethiopia at the Venice Biennale, for its 60th edition in 2024, bringing to an international stage a visual language forged in migration – one that speaks directly to the experience of being from somewhere while constantly negotiating that origin from elsewhere. The lingering departure is not merely a theme in his art so much as the condition of his life."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tesfaye-Urgessa-Sternschnuppen-2025-2026_4.jpeg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Sternschnuppen by Tesfaye Urgessa, Oil on canvas, 200 × 180 cm, 2025-2026. © Tesfaye Urgessa. Photo: © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This sensibility is evident in works like Sternschnuppen (2025-26), the title of which comes from the German for shooting stars, evoking transcience, wonder and the act of making a wish. In the painting, a mother-like figure shelters two smaller figures beneath her. The scene suggests a picnic, with the figures resting atop a white cloth on the ground, on which abstract forms – resembling bits of toys and limbs – stand in for bread or fruit, transforming a personal memory into a universal image of rest and protection. “It becomes less about a particular family activity and more about a universal image of rest, togetherness and protection,” says Urgessa."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tesfaye-Urgessa-War-in-Play-2025_3.jpeg?resize=768%2C1024&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "War in Play by Tesfaye Urgessa, Oil on canvas, 250 × 200 cm, 2025. © Tesfaye Urgessa. Photo: © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Similarly, in War in Play (2025), a female figure becomes a kind of shelter, absorbing danger before it reaches the children enveloped beneath her blue mantle. From the right side of the composition, hands throw small, plane-like objects into the space, a gesture that recalls the innocence of childhood paper aeroplanes but here carries a darker resonance. The mother figure’s mouth is open, ready to swallow one of these objects, consuming the danger before it can reach those she protects. “I cannot avoid thinking about the way governments and political leaders sometimes appear to play with objects of enormous destructive power as if they were toys,” he says. “The consequences fall upon people who have very little power over the decisions being made: children, mothers, the elderly, the sick.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The domestic interiors that recur in his work, such as in Of What Once Was (2026) and Safe Slumber (2025), are psychologically charged, not through deliberate design but through the act of painting itself. “When you deny some of the natural laws that we normally understand – such as perspective, gravity or the way objects are supposed to occupy space – and begin to break those laws, a certain tension happens almost automatically,” he says."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Distinctively elongated bodies take central position, often kneeling or sitting, brushing up against the limits of the frame. In Of What Once Was , a female figure’s back swells into an enormous arc that encloses a tangle of limbs from a quartet of figures clustered at the composition’s centre, imparting a sense of motion. “I am drawn to the idea that the figures are not simply suspended in a room but are travelling through time and space,” explains Urgessa. “Perhaps the floating figures are moving away from what once defined them. Perhaps they are simply passing through another state. I am more interested in leaving them suspended in that uncertain space: between what once was and what they are becoming.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i0.wp.com/artomity.art/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Tesfaye-Urgessa-Of-what-once-was-2026_1.jpeg?resize=840%2C630&ssl=1", "alt": "", "caption": "Of what once was by Tesfaye Urgessa, Oil on canvas, 270 × 260 cm, 2026.© Tesfaye Urgessa. Photo: © White Cube (Kitmin Lee).", "credit": "Artomity"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The surfaces of Urgessa’s canvases are a record of his process, where rough, gestural marks sit alongside refined, deliberate passages. Certain elements to which the artist wants to draw attention are exaggerated with colour and texture. “In the beginning of a painting, I tend to work very fast, impulsively and gesturally. But as the painting develops, that speed gradually gets replaced by more thinking, slowing down and working within smaller areas, with greater attention to detail,” he says. The tension between spontaneity and control is not premeditated but emerges organically. This approach mirrors the thematic tensions in his work of intimacy and distance, home and migration, individual identity and collective life."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Hong Kong, a city itself defined by movement and transition, this resonance feels particularly acute. Urgessa’s figures, caught between departure and belonging, speak directly to the feeling of being suspended between worlds. “We move from childhood into adolescence, from adolescence into adulthood; we live in one place and then leave it for another; we become one thing and then transition into something else,” he says. “What remains through these transitions, and how little of what we once were can remain with us continuously, is perhaps a trace, a memory or a fragment of a previous state.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Urgessa’s paintings, leaving is never a clean break. It remains emotionally unresolved – a condition rather than an event. The Lingering Departure asks what we carry with us, what we leave behind and how memory travels with us into the present and beyond."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在香港白立方乾淨潔白的展覽空間裡，特斯法耶・烏爾蓋薩的新作彷彿散發著一股內斂的強烈張力。一群群人物從層層疊疊的畫面中浮現，既像凝固在原地，又彷彿仍在移動，棲身於室內空間與混亂的群像場景之中。畫布上，粗獷而原始的筆觸與經過細緻琢磨的部分刻意形成張力。是次展覽「未決之離」是烏爾蓋薩自8月加入畫廊後的首個展覽。此前，他剛於北京紅磚美術館舉行在亞洲的首次博物館個展，展覽匯聚他過去一年在亞的斯亞貝巴及斯圖加特創作的作品。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "「未決之離」取自其中一幅作品的標題，捕捉了烏爾蓋薩創作的情感核心。離開從來不是一個單一的時刻，而是一種在啟程之前便已開始、抵達之後仍久久延續的狀態。烏爾蓋薩從德國的工作室以電郵回覆：「『離開』聽起來很突然，而『未決』則暗示留存。」他指出：「在任何身體或心理變化發生之前，都會有一段等待的時間。然後離開發生了，但你離開的地方並不會因此消失，它會透過記憶與你同行。」"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他在埃塞俄比亞度過童年並接受藝術訓練，其後移居德國，如今又在不同洲份之間展開創作。這條貫穿人生的軌跡，讓藝術家所說「你離開的地方並不會消失」這句話更具重量。烏爾蓋薩於1983年在亞的斯亞貝巴出生，從小看著父親以鄰居相片作依歸繪畫肖像，在一個藝術融入生活的家庭中長大。他說：「看著他畫畫，讓我從小時候便開始對畫畫產生興趣。但直到青少年後期，我才真正知道原來有一整個藝術世界的存在，而藝術家可以是一種職業。」"}, article_text:
In the sterile, white-walled space of White Cube Hong Kong, Tesfaye Urgessa’s new paintings seem to radiate a contained intensity. Clusters of figures emerge from layered surfaces at once frozen and in motion, inhabiting interiors and chaotic tableaux. Across the canvas, rough, raw marks sit in deliberate tension with passages of refined detail. The exhibition, The Lingering Departure , marks Urgessa’s first show with the gallery since joining in August. It follows his first solo museum presentation in Asia, at the Red Brick Art Museum in Beijing, and brings together works created over the past year in Addis Ababa and Stuttgart.

Taken from one of the paintings’ titles, The Lingering Departure captures the emotional core of Urgessa’s practice, the idea that leaving is never reduced to a single moment but is a state that begins before departure and continues long after arrival. “A departure sounds sudden, while lingering suggests something that remains,” emails Urgessa from his studio in Germany. “Before any physical or psychological change happens, there is a period of anticipation. Then the departure takes place but the place you left does not disappear. It stays with you through memory.”

A biographical arc of childhood and art training in Ethiopia, migration to Germany and now a practice that moves between continents gives weight to the artist’s assertion that the place you left does not disappear. Born in Addis Ababa in 1983, Urgessa grew up in a family where art was woven into the quotidian, watching his father draw portraits from photographs of neighbours. “I think seeing him draw and paint created an interest in me to start drawing myself when I was very young,” he says. “But I didn’t really know, until quite late in my teenage years, that there was a whole world of art or that becoming an artist could actually be a profession.”

His early visual education came not from galleries or textbooks but from copying the flat, vivid figures of Ethiopian Orthodox church murals, an experience that embedded a distinct way of seeing into his work. “The frontal gaze of the figures, the vivid and bright colours but also the simplicity and flatness of the compositions – those qualities stayed with me visually,” he explains.

It was only later, at art school in Ethiopia and then in Germany, where he enrolled at the State Academy of Fine Arts Stuttgart in 2009, that he encountered a wider art history, sharpening the questions of identity that had previously remained unspoken and would become foundational to his practice. “I don’t really remember thinking about my identity in the same way before I came to Germany,” he admits. “Being in a different country and culture made me much more aware of where I came from and how I was perceived by others.”

The physical departure from Addis Ababa did not erase Ethiopia; instead, it became a psychological presence that travelled with him, refracted through memory, language and the politics of belonging in Europe. As migration grew, these questions grew louder in his work. “It made me think more deeply about migration, belonging, exclusion and the way societies decide who belongs and who does not,” he says.

Yet the paintings avoid falling into didacticism: they are not illustrations of political arguments but spaces in which psychological and social tensions coexist. Urgessa’s figures, often suspended in kinetic, dense compositions where objects and figures coexist alongside one another, seem to embody this condition of being neither fully rooted nor entirely adrift, existing in a liminal space shaped by displacement. It was fitting, then, that he was the first artist to represent Ethiopia at the Venice Biennale, for its 60th edition in 2024, bringing to an international stage a visual language forged in migration – one that speaks directly to the experience of being from somewhere while constantly negotiating that origin from elsewhere. The lingering departure is not merely a theme in his art so much as the condition of his life.

This sensibility is evident in works like Sternschnuppen (2025-26), the title of which comes from the German for shooting stars, evoking transcience, wonder and the act of making a wish. In the painting, a mother-like figure shelters two smaller figures beneath her. The scene suggests a picnic, with the figures resting atop a white cloth on the ground, on which abstract forms – resembling bits of toys and limbs – stand in for bread or fruit, transforming a personal memory into a universal image of rest and protection. “It becomes less about a particular family activity and more about a universal image of rest, togetherness and protection,” says Urgessa.

Similarly, in War in Play (2025), a female figure becomes a kind of shelter, absorbing danger before it reaches the children enveloped beneath her blue mantle. From the right side of the composition, hands throw small, plane-like objects into the space, a gesture that recalls the innocence of childhood paper aeroplanes but here carries a darker resonance. The mother figure’s mouth is open, ready to swallow one of these objects, consuming the danger before it can reach those she protects. “I cannot avoid thinking about the way governments and political leaders sometimes appear to play with objects of enormous destructive power as if they were toys,” he says. “The consequences fall upon people who have very little power over the decisions being made: children, mothers, the elderly, the sick.”

The domestic interiors that recur in his work, such as in Of What Once Was (2026) and Safe Slumber (2025), are psychologically charged, not through deliberate design but through the act of painting itself. “When you deny some of the natural laws that we normally understand – such as perspective, gravity or the way objects are supposed to occupy space – and begin to break those laws, a certain tension happens almost automatically,” he says.

Distinctively elongated bodies take central position, often kneeling or sitting, brushing up against the limits of the frame. In Of What Once Was , a female figure’s back swells into an enormous arc that encloses a tangle of limbs from a quartet of figures clustered at the composition’s centre, imparting a sense of motion. “I am drawn to the idea that the figures are not simply suspended in a room but are travelling through time and space,” explains Urgessa. “Perhaps the floating figures are moving away from what once defined them. Perhaps they are simply passing through another state. I am more interested in leaving them suspended in that uncertain space: between what once was and what they are becoming.”

The surfaces of Urgessa’s canvases are a record of his process, where rough, gestural marks sit alongside refined, deliberate passages. Certain elements to which the artist wants to draw attention are exaggerated with colour and texture. “In the beginning of a painting, I tend to work very fast, impulsively and gesturally. But as the painting develops, that speed gradually gets replaced by more thinking, slowing down and working within smaller areas, with greater attention to detail,” he says. The tension between spontaneity and control is not premeditated but emerges organically. This approach mirrors the thematic tensions in his work of intimacy and distance, home and migration, individual identity and collective life.

In Hong Kong, a city itself defined by movement and transition, this resonance feels particularly acute. Urgessa’s figures, caught between departure and belonging, speak directly to the feeling of being suspended between worlds. “We move from childhood into adolescence, from adolescence into adulthood; we live in one place and then leave it for another; we become one thing and then transition into something else,” he says. “What remains through these transitions, and how little of what we once were can remain with us continuously, is perhaps a trace, a memory or a fragment of a previous state.”

In Urgessa’s paintings, leaving is never a clean break. It remains emotionally unresolved – a condition rather than an event. The Lingering Departure asks what we carry with us, what we leave behind and how memory travels with us into the present and beyond.

在香港白立方乾淨潔白的展覽空間裡，特斯法耶・烏爾蓋薩的新作彷彿散發著一股內斂的強烈張力。一群群人物從層層疊疊的畫面中浮現，既像凝固在原地，又彷彿仍在移動，棲身於室內空間與混亂的群像場景之中。畫布上，粗獷而原始的筆觸與經過細緻琢磨的部分刻意形成張力。是次展覽「未決之離」是烏爾蓋薩自8月加入畫廊後的首個展覽。此前，他剛於北京紅磚美術館舉行在亞洲的首次博物館個展，展覽匯聚他過去一年在亞的斯亞貝巴及斯圖加特創作的作品。

「未決之離」取自其中一幅作品的標題，捕捉了烏爾蓋薩創作的情感核心。離開從來不是一個單一的時刻，而是一種在啟程之前便已開始、抵達之後仍久久延續的狀態。烏爾蓋薩從德國的工作室以電郵回覆：「『離開』聽起來很突然，而『未決』則暗示留存。」他指出：「在任何身體或心理變化發生之前，都會有一段等待的時間。然後離開發生了，但你離開的地方並不會因此消失，它會透過記憶與你同行。」

他在埃塞俄比亞度過童年並接受藝術訓練，其後移居德國，如今又在不同洲份之間展開創作。這條貫穿人生的軌跡，讓藝術家所說「你離開的地方並不會消失」這句話更具重量。烏爾蓋薩於1983年在亞的斯亞貝巴出生，從小看著父親以鄰居相片作依歸繪畫肖像，在一個藝術融入生活的家庭中長大。他說：「看著他畫畫，讓我從小時候便開始對畫畫產生興趣。但直到青少年後期，我才真正知道原來有一整個藝術世界的存在，而藝術家可以是一種職業。」

他早期的視覺教育並非來自畫廊或教科書，而是來自臨摹埃塞俄比亞東正教教堂壁畫中平面而鮮明的人物，這段經歷將一種獨特的觀看方式植入他的創作之中。他解釋道：「人物正面凝視的方式、鮮明明亮的色彩，以及構圖的簡潔與平面感，這些特質在視覺上一直留在我心裡。」

直到後來在埃塞俄比亞的藝術學校，以及其後於2009年入讀德國斯圖加特國立造型藝術學院，他才接觸到更廣闊的藝術史，亦開始更清晰地思考過去一直未曾言明、後來成為其創作根基的身份問題。他坦言：「我來德國之前，未曾以同樣的方式思考自己的身份。身處一個不同的國家和文化之中，讓我更加意識到自己來自哪裡，以及別人如何看待自己。

離開亞的斯亞貝巴的經驗並沒有抹去埃塞俄比亞，相反，它化為了一種同行的心理存在，透過記憶、語言，以及歐洲社會中關於歸屬的政治折射出來。隨著移民經歷逐漸加深，這些問題也在他的作品中變得愈來愈鮮明。他說：「這讓我更深入地思考移民、歸屬、排斥，以及社會如何決定誰屬於這裡、誰不屬於這裡。」

然而，這些畫作並沒有落入說教式的表達，它們並不是政治論述的圖解，而是讓心理與社會張力共存的空間。烏爾蓋薩筆下的人物經常懸置於充滿動感而密集的構圖之中，物件與人物彼此並置，彷彿體現出一種既未完全扎根、又未徹底漂泊的狀態，存在於由離散所塑造的臨界空間。他成為2024年第60屆威尼斯雙年展首位代表埃塞俄比亞參展的藝術家，也就再恰當不過。他將一種在移居經驗中形成的視覺語言帶到國際舞台，這種語言直接回應了身為某個地方的人、卻又不斷從另一個地方重新協商自身出身的經驗。這種揮之不去的別離不只是他藝術中的一個主題，更幾乎是他生命本身的狀態。

這種感受在《Sternschnuppen》（2025–26年）等作品中尤其明顯。作品標題取自德語，意為「流星」，令人聯想到轉瞬即逝、驚奇，以及許願的行為。畫中，一名如母親般的人物庇護著身下兩個較小的人物。場景似乎是野餐，人物坐臥於地上的白布之上，而布上散落著抽象形體，形似玩具碎片與四肢的物體取代了麵包和水果，將個人記憶轉化為一幅關於休憩與保護的普世圖像。烏爾蓋薩說：「它不只是關於某個特定家庭活動，而更像是一幅關於休息、相聚與保護的普世圖像。」

同樣地，在《War in Play》（2025年）中，一名女性人物成為某種庇護，在危險觸及被她藍色披肩包覆的孩子之前，先將危險承擔。構圖右側有多隻手將形似飛機的小物拋入空間，動作令人想起童年摺紙飛機的天真爛漫，但在此卻帶有更陰暗的意味。母親般的人物張開嘴巴，準備吞下其中一件物體，在危險觸及她所保護的人之前先將它吞噬。他說：「我不禁想起政府與政治領袖有時彷彿把擁有巨大毀滅力量的東西當成玩具般戲弄。後果卻落在那些對相關決策幾乎沒有任何影響力的兒童、母親、老人，以及病患者身上。」

他的作品如《Of What Once Was》（2026年）與《Safe Slumber》（2025年）中反覆出現家庭室內空間，其心理張力並非來自刻意的設計，而是源於繪畫本身的行為。他說：「當你否定一些我們通常理解的自然法則，例如透視、重力，或物件理應如何佔據空間，並開始打破這些法則時，某種張力幾乎會自然產生。」

在其畫作中，別具特色地比例修長的人體佔據畫面中央，往往跪著或坐著，身體幾乎觸及畫框的邊界。在《Of What Once Was》裡，一名女性人物的背部隆起成巨大的弧形，包圍著構圖中央四名人物交纏的四肢，營造出一種動態。烏爾蓋薩解釋道：「我著迷於人物並非只是懸浮在一個房間裡，而是在時間與空間之中移動的這個想法。也許那些漂浮的人物正逐漸遠離曾經定義他們的事物，只是在經歷另一種狀態。我更感興趣的是讓他們停留在那個不確定的空間裡，介乎曾經的自己與正在成為的自己之間。」

烏爾蓋薩的畫布表面記錄了他的創作過程，粗獷、帶有動勢的筆觸與細緻而經過刻意處理的部分並置。一些藝術家希望觀者注意的元素，會透過色彩與質感加以誇張。他說：「一幅畫剛開始時，我通常畫得非常快，帶著衝動與動勢。但隨著畫作逐漸發展，這種速度會慢慢被更多思考所取代。我會放慢下來，在較小的區域裡創作，更加注重細節。」自發與控制之間的張力並非事先計劃，而是在創作過程中自然浮現。這種方式也映照了他作品中的主題張力：親密與距離、家園與移民、個人身份與集體生活。

在香港這座本身便由流動與轉變所定義的城市裡，這種共鳴顯得格外強烈。烏爾蓋薩筆下那些被困在離開與歸屬之間的人物，直接訴說著一種懸置於不同世界之間的感受。「我們從童年走向青春期，從青春期走向成年。我們生活在一個地方，然後離開它前往另一個地方。我們成為某種人，然後又轉變成另一種人。」他說。「在這些轉變之中，究竟有甚麼能夠留下來，而我們曾經是誰，又有多少能夠一直與我們同行？也許留下來的，只是一道痕跡、一段記憶，或某個過去狀態的碎片。」

在烏爾蓋薩的畫作中，離開從來不是一次乾脆利落的割裂。它始終處於未完結的情感狀態之中。與其說是一件事件，不如說是一種狀態。「未決之離」追問的是：我們會帶著甚麼同行、又會將甚麼留在身後，以及記憶如何隨我們進入當下，並繼續走向更遠的地方。

editorial_excerpt_zh: 所谓的“DC宇宙”目前已经推出了三部电影——但到目前为止，这一品牌似乎除了最死忠的nerd之外，并未真正破圈。去年的《超人》重启版还算体面，今年夏天的《女超人》略逊一筹，不过，将它们连接起来的更大故事世界的宏大前景……

article_text:
We are now three movies into the so-called DC Universe — branding that so far doesn’t appear to have cut through to any but the most devoted of nerds. Last year’s “Superman” reboot was respectable enough, this summer’s “Supergirl” a bit less so, but the prospect of a larger story world connecting them hardly sets the pulse racing. A comparatively obscure comic-book adaptation, “ Clayface ” is considerably more interesting all round, in large part because it doesn’t yet feel bound to any superhero property. Tonally and stylistically, this nasty, gnarly body-horror movie is its own ugly animal; perhaps the characters and conflicts introduced here would pall if given the franchise treatment, but in the context of a single, genre-melding romp, they’re fresh and ickily enjoyable.

Netflix Shocker: Bela Bajaria Leaving After 10 Years Amid Layoffs, Peter Rice to Replace as Chief Content Officer

The character history of Clayface is long and imprecise, taking different names and incarnations through an assortment of DC Comics products over the last 86 years — absolutely zero knowledge of which is required to watch “Clayface.” Mike Flanagan’s story loosely co-opts the villain origin tale behind many of those incarnations — actor with an ax to grind gains shapeshifting abilities — but otherwise starts more or less from scratch. The film, directed with good humor and a healthy sense of the grotesque by reliable British genre craftsman James Watkins (“Eden Lake,” “Speak No Evil”), is as indebted to cartoonish ’90s horror outings like “Darkman” and “Thinner” as it is to anything in its own direct franchise history. Right down to its grisly practical makeup effects, it’s a pleasing throwback.

It’s fitting that the role of Matt Hagen, a young actor taken down just as he hits the big time, is cast with a face we don’t yet know by heart. Best known for U.K. indies like “Effi o Blaenau” and a supporting role in Guy Ritchie’s “The Gentlemen,” the Welsh actor Tom Rhys Harries brings the requisite sandy handsomeness to proceedings, but also an anguished hunger: You can believe he’d do just about anything to regain the chance that has slipped through his fingers once before.

When we meet Matt, being limo-driven to set in the bronzing sunlight of Coast City (that’s DC-speak for Los Angeles), he’s on the verge of becoming a household name, charming the talk-show circuit in the wake of his first Oscar nomination. But he’s still reasonably grounded, spending much of his free time hanging out with less successful actor bestie Corey (Joshua James), and capable of bad behavior that a good publicist wouldn’t countenance — like a nightclub hookup with young honey-trap starlet Mia (Joana Ribeiro), who just happens to be the girlfriend of fearsome Gotham City mobster Szabo (David Dencik). Bad move: The next morning, a thoroughly displeased Szabo takes to Matt’s million-dollar face with a switchblade, and the ensuing career downturn (with a timely side of cancel culture) is quick and precipitous.

A victim of an industry that takes its stars literally at face value, the now-destitute Matt is desperate to repair his ruined mug — which is where experimental scientist Dr. Caitlyn Corr ( Naomi Ackie ) comes in. She’s developing a cellular replacement technology for degenerative diseases, still very much in the untested phase; he’s all too willing to be her guinea pig. The early results are miraculous, as his face repairs itself to its previous dreamboat state in a matter of months; unluckily for him, his cells are loath to leave things there. For Dr. Corr is above all else a practitioner of movie science, and soon enough, for no rational reason whatsoever, Matt’s face can take on an unpredictable array of forms, both human and monstrous — with violent consequences for those who have crossed him along the way.

It goes without saying that this is all piping-hot nonsense, but in nearly every department, “Clayface” exceeds expectations — all without getting ideas above its spiritual B-movie station. The script is several notches slicker and slyer than most in this genre lane, thanks to the elegant, lightly ironic touch of Hossein Amini (“Drive,” “The Wings of the Dove”), whose pithy dialogue gives the film’s criminal confrontations some bite, and the requisite romantic stirrings between doctor and patient a bit of crackle.

It helps that the reliably resourceful Ackie gives Caitlyn more curiosity and conscience than the sexy-scientist archetype typically permits, while classy, imaginative casting pays off throughout the ensemble: Max Minghella brings a witty squareness, straight out of midcentury comic-book noir, to the thankless role of Caitlyn’s suspicious cop boyfriend, while Dencik does hair-trigger villain duty with genuinely unnerving levels of sleaze.

This all gives solid (more or less) real-world grounding to the wilder body-horror antics that we’re really here for, and “Clayface” more than delivers the goods on that front. Abetted by consistently inspired prosthetics work, there’s enough stomach-churning, actually face-melting corporeal silly-putty play here to make sense of the film’s Halloween-friendly release date, and at least one dynamite gross-out setpiece — involving fused eyelids, nail scissors and a brutal bout of plane turbulence — that will fuel nightmares well into the coming months.

It’s one of many scenes directed by Watkins with the sadistic glee of a filmmaker handed the rare freedom of an R rating for his comic-book antics: Unconcerned with pleasing the broadest possible crowd, the film is odd, oozy fun, both as juvenile and as adult as it needs to be. If we must have a DC Universe, it could use more movies like this one — just not, you know, exactly like it, rebooted into oblivion. For now, at least, “Clayface” is made to its own mold.

With: Tom Rhys Harries, Naomi Ackie, David Dencik, Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan, Joshua James, Joana Ribeiro.

title_original: Frank Lloyd Wright’s Taliesin West Home in Arizona Temporarily Closes After a Man Dies
editorial_title_zh: 弗兰克·劳埃德·赖特位于亚利桑那州的西塔里森住宅在一名男子身亡后临时关闭
editorial_excerpt_zh: 周五，一名男子在参加徒步导览时于该物业遭遇离奇事故身亡。

article_text:
Frank Lloyd Wright ’s Taliesin West home in Scottsdale, Arizona, is temporarily closing after a man died on the property on Friday during a walking tour, reported local news channel AZ Family .

The individual was identified to be Rogério Renato Mateucci, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná. According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, the incident took place at 2 p.m. local time, where Mateucci was struck by roofing material dislodged by strong winds while he was on a group walking tour. Mateucci died instantly and the death is being treated as a weather-related accident.

At the time of the incident, local television channels had reported that it was a First Alert Weather Day, where weather teams warn viewers of upcoming events that may disrupt travel or safety. The National Weather Service reported east winds of 22 miles per hour in the area with gusts up to 32 miles per hour. No injuries or other deaths have been reported in regards to the other individuals on the walking tour.

The foundation’s CEO, Joe Spector, told AZ Family that the foundation “extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the individual” and that “no further details will be shared out of respect for privacy and to allow officials to complete their work.” On Instagram, the foundation wrote that the “Scottsdale Police Department is aware of the incident” and that the property is “closed to the public until further notice.”

Wright built the studio and home in 1937 and lived there until his death in 1959. The property spans across 491 acres. In 1940, New York’s Museum of Modern Art exhibited a complex of the property, and then in 1947, pictures of the structures were displayed.
excerpt_original: A a man died of a freak accident on the property on Friday during a walking tour.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/6dbcea64/0c974ef3-d527-4bd3-8363-19e6b0d5486a.jpeg?w=2352&q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "阿赖耶在表参道开启的东京新篇章", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴黎时装屋“阿赖耶（Alaïa）”于10月15日在东京表参道开设了快闪空间。这是阿赖耶首次在表参道呈现品牌的世界观，该快闪店也是常设旗舰店开业前的先导项目。展期将持续至3月31日。在汇聚了时尚、艺术与建筑的表参道会场中，展出了摄影师北岛敬三的摄影装置《Index 0》。此外，品牌还与东京本土的艺术书专业分销商“twelvebooks”达成合作，店内陈列了专为本次快闪店策划的精选书籍。不仅如此，为纪念开业，现场还备好了专为本次快闪店准备的成衣与配饰，让来访者能够亲身体验品牌的独特世界观。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/73e2bf29/58a3a2b7-6d91-4da7-9a0a-389bbe3fd495.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌中专为本次快闪店策划的书籍", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "在巴黎大秀上首次亮相的《Index 0》", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Index 0》是3月在巴黎发布的Summer Fall 2026系列时装秀上首次亮相的作品。对担任创意总监长达5年的彼得·穆里尔（Pieter Mulier）而言，该系列是他在阿赖耶的最后一场大秀。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/f07b53d9/f6c3e5a7-d46e-42fc-91d7-2fbc096d4277.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌，除成衣外，阿赖耶标志性的手袋“Le Teckel”也一应俱全", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "以使用大画幅相机的肖像摄影系列《PORTRAITS》等闻名、并于2022年凭借摄影集《UNTITLED RECORDS》荣获第41届土门拳奖的北岛，在此次作品中拍摄了构成阿赖耶核心的人物。精品店内的全景屏幕上，放映着这些人物沉浸式的肖像。作品中捕捉到的他们的双手、举止与执着态度，正是塑造阿赖耶特质的重要元素。通过坦诚而亲密地捕捉他们不加掩饰的身影，该作品向个体创作背后的集体精神以及创造过程原点处的人性致以敬意。何不在展场中感受一下支撑阿赖耶产品制造的人们的真实面貌呢。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/6dbcea64/0c974ef3-d527-4bd3-8363-19e6b0d5486a.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "展场风貌", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/6dbcea64/0c974ef3-d527-4bd3-8363-19e6b0d5486a.jpeg?w=2352&q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "アライアが表参道で開く、東京での新たな章"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "パリのファッションメゾンである「アライア（Alaïa）」は、10月15日に東京・表参道でポップアップスペースをオープンした。アライアが表参道でメゾンの世界観を展開するのは今回が初めてで、本ポップアップは常設のフラッグシップストア開業に先がけたものとなる。会期は3月31日まで。 ファッションやアート、建築が行き交う表参道の会場では、写真家・ 北島敬三 によるフォトグラフィック・インスタレーション《Index 0》を展示している。あわせて、東京を拠点とするアートブック専門のディストリビューター「twelvebooks」とパートナーシップを結び、本ポップアップのために特別にキュレーションされた書籍を店内に揃えた。さらにオープンを記念して、本ポップアップのために用意されたプレタポルテやアクセサリーも並び、来場者はメゾンの世界観を体感できる。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/73e2bf29/58a3a2b7-6d91-4da7-9a0a-389bbe3fd495.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景より、本ポップアップのために特別にキュレーションされた書籍", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "パリのショーで初披露された《Index 0》"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Index 0》は、パリで3月に発表されたSummer Fall 2026コレクションのショーで初めて披露された作品。このコレクションは、5年にわたりクリエイティブ・ディレクターを務めた ピーター・ミュリエ にとってアライアでの最後のショーとなった。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/f07b53d9/f6c3e5a7-d46e-42fc-91d7-2fbc096d4277.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景より、プレタポルテとあわせて、アライアのアイコニックなバッグ「ル・テケル」も揃う", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大判カメラによる肖像写真のシリーズ「PORTRAITS」などで知られ、2022年に写真集『UNTITLED RECORDS』で第41回土門拳賞を受賞した北島は、本作でアライアの中核を担う人々を撮影した。ブティック内のパノラマスクリーンには、彼らの没入感のある肖像が映し出される。作品にとらえられた彼らの手や仕草、ひたむきな姿勢は、アライアのアイデンティティをかたち作る大切な要素である。飾らない姿を率直かつ親密にとらえた肖像を通して、本作は個々のクリエーションの背景にある集合的な精神と、創造のプロセスの原点にある人間性を讃えている。アライアのものづくりを支える人々の素顔に、会場で触れてみてはいかがだろうか。"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://cdn.prod.tabdev.net/asset_files/uploaded/2026-10/6dbcea64/0c974ef3-d527-4bd3-8363-19e6b0d5486a.jpeg?q=70&fm=webp", "alt": "", "caption": "会場風景", "credit": "Tokyo Art Beat"}]
article_text:
アライアが表参道で開く、東京での新たな章

パリのファッションメゾンである「アライア（Alaïa）」は、10月15日に東京・表参道でポップアップスペースをオープンした。アライアが表参道でメゾンの世界観を展開するのは今回が初めてで、本ポップアップは常設のフラッグシップストア開業に先がけたものとなる。会期は3月31日まで。 ファッションやアート、建築が行き交う表参道の会場では、写真家・ 北島敬三 によるフォトグラフィック・インスタレーション《Index 0》を展示している。あわせて、東京を拠点とするアートブック専門のディストリビューター「twelvebooks」とパートナーシップを結び、本ポップアップのために特別にキュレーションされた書籍を店内に揃えた。さらにオープンを記念して、本ポップアップのために用意されたプレタポルテやアクセサリーも並び、来場者はメゾンの世界観を体感できる。

パリのショーで初披露された《Index 0》

《Index 0》は、パリで3月に発表されたSummer Fall 2026コレクションのショーで初めて披露された作品。このコレクションは、5年にわたりクリエイティブ・ディレクターを務めた ピーター・ミュリエ にとってアライアでの最後のショーとなった。

大判カメラによる肖像写真のシリーズ「PORTRAITS」などで知られ、2022年に写真集『UNTITLED RECORDS』で第41回土門拳賞を受賞した北島は、本作でアライアの中核を担う人々を撮影した。ブティック内のパノラマスクリーンには、彼らの没入感のある肖像が映し出される。作品にとらえられた彼らの手や仕草、ひたむきな姿勢は、アライアのアイデンティティをかたち作る大切な要素である。飾らない姿を率直かつ親密にとらえた肖像を通して、本作は個々のクリエーションの背景にある集合的な精神と、創造のプロセスの原点にある人間性を讃えている。アライアのものづくりを支える人々の素顔に、会場で触れてみてはいかがだろうか。

article_text:
Filming on Miami Vice ’85 was disrupted on Friday night when a man threatened a member of the production with a butcher knife.

According to an NYPD spokesperson, 23-year-old Alex Perez of Brooklyn was arrested at around 11:15pm on charges of menacing and criminal possession of a weapon after police were called to the vicinity of Avenue N and McDonald Avenue.

A member of the production team told police that Perez drew the knife after a verbal dispute, “causing him to become fearful for his safety.”

Everything We Know About Universal’s ‘Miami Vice ’85’ Movie So Far

‘Miami Vice ’85’ First Look: See Austin Butler & Michael B. Jordan As Crockett & Tubbs

Perez was taken into custody and the knife was recovered with no injuries. Deadline has reached out to Universal for a comment.

Filming began this month on Miami Vice ’85 around New Jersey and New York City, where Michael B. Jordan has been seen shooting in character as Ricardo Tubbs.

Watch on Deadline

Last year, Universal set a reboot of the 1980s NBC series from director Joseph Kosinski and a script by Dan Gilroy and Eric Warren Singer. Jordan was cast as Tubbs in the movie, with Austin Butler taking on the role of Sonny Crockett .

The cast also includes Alden Ehrenreich, Whitney Peak, Camila Morrone, Danny Ramirez, John Leguizamo, Andrew Schulz, Walton Goggins, André Holland, Michael Irby and Haley Lu Richardson.

article_text:
Museum Ludwig traces the overlooked connections between the Black diaspora and European modernism, revealing a transatlantic history shaped by movement, exchange and resistance.

What happens to modernism when you view its history across the Atlantic? Marking Museum Ludwig’s 50th anniversary, ‘Along the Color Line: Traces of a Transatlantic Modernism’ brings modern and contemporary artists of the Black diaspora into dialogue with works from the museum’s collection.

Taking its title from the writings of African American sociologist W. E. B. Du Bois, the exhibition examines the cultural exchanges, migrations and encounters that connected Black artistic practice with European modernism. Painting, sculpture, drawing, literature and music reveal a history shaped by movements including the Harlem Renaissance and Négritude.

Curated by Eboa Itondo, the exhibition also confronts the historic absence of Black artists within European museum collections. Artists including Mildred Thompson, Herbert Gentry and Iba Ndiaye offer alternative perspectives on modernism, while James Gregory Atkinson’s nonlinear archive connects early twentieth-century histories with contemporary Black diasporic experience.

Moving between continents and generations, ‘Along the Colour Line’ reveals the intercultural relationships often obscured in established art histories, inviting audiences to reconsider modernism through questions of identity, community, migration, and belonging.

This exhibition is on view at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne until 7 March 2027.

article_text:
Daniel Kaluuya will make his New York stage debut in “ Grass ,” a new play from Tony Award- and Pulitzer Prize-winner Branden Jacobs-Jenkins .

“Grass” traces a mother and son’s surreal, sprawling road trip through the American South marked by fantastical encounters with historical and allegorical figures. A press release describes “Grass” as “equal parts fantasia, memory play, and morality play” and a “surreal meditation on the limits of personal, ancestral, and national identity amidst social upheaval.” The play will have its world premiere Off Broadway at Park Avenue Armory, with opening night set for Feb. 26.

Related Stories

Ava DuVernay on Her Latest Doc '14th': 'We're in the Midst of Something Very Sinister, Something Very Dangerous'

Jacobs-Jenkins is the playwright behind Broadway hits including “Appropriate,” which starred Sarah Paulson, Corey Stoll, Natalie Gold, Elle Fanning and Alyssa Emily Marvin, and “Purpose,” led by Jon Michael Hill, LaTanya Richardson Jackson, Harry Lennix and Kara Young. “Appropriate” was nominated for eight Tonys and won three, including best revival. “Purpose” was nominated for six Tonys and won two, including best play.

Kaluuya won an Oscar for Shaka King’s 2021 Fred Hampton biopic “Judas and the Black Messiah.” The British actor broke out in 2017’s Oscar-nominated “Get Out” and went on to star in movies such as “Black Panther,” Steve McQueen’s crime drama “Widows,” Jordan Peele’s “Nope,” Sony’s “Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse” and Chris Rock’s “Misty Green.” He’s also currently developing a live-action “Barney” movie for A24 and Mattel. On stage, Kaluuya appeared in several London productions including “Oxford Street,” “Sucker Punch,” “A Season in the Congo” and “Blue/Orange.”

“Grass” reunites Jacobs-Jenkins with director Sarah Benson and set designer Mimi Lien, who worked on his 2014 play “An Octoroon.” The creative team includes lighting designer Jane Cox and Stacey Derosier, sound designer Bray Poor, special effects designer Jeremy Chernick, costume designer Enver Chakartash and wig and makeup designer Cookie Jordan.

article_text:
ニューヨークを拠点に活動する写真家、アダム・パウエル（Adam Powell）の世界初個展「The DESERT is a CIRCLE」が、2026年11月14日（土）から2027年1月11日（月・祝）まで、東京・渋谷のDIESEL ART GALLERYで開催される。

イングランド・エセックス出身のパウエルは、現実を観察して捉えた写真と、演出によって構築された写真を横断し、その境界を曖昧にする表現を追求してきた。時間や反復、商業、アメリカーナなどをテーマに、自ら被写体として登場するセルフポートレートも制作。音楽やファッションの分野でも活動し、Blood OrangeやWater From Your Eyesのアーティスト写真をはじめ、DIESEL、Salomon、i-D、SSENSEなどの仕事を手がけている。

本展では、人影のない風景やハイウェイ、モーテルを通り抜けながら、砂漠を横断する旅を描く。移り変わる風景や夜ごとに異なるモーテルの部屋、時折写真の中に姿を現すパウエル自身。旅が進むにつれて時間の感覚は薄れ、現実と幻想の境界が曖昧になっていく。

明確な始まりも終わりもなく、どこまでも続く道。記録と演出、現実と虚構を交錯させながら、熱に浮かされた夢のような世界へと鑑賞者を誘う展覧会となる。

会場では、DIESELとのコラボレーションTシャツ（税込15,400円）をはじめとする限定グッズも販売。Tシャツは11月13日（金）18時から、DIESEL SHIBUYAおよび公式オンラインストアで発売される。

タイトル

アダム・パウエル「The DESERT is a CIRCLE」

場所

DIESEL ART GALLERY（東京都渋谷区渋谷1-23-16 cocoti DIESEL SHIBUYA B1F）

会期

2026年11月14日（土）〜2027年1月11日（月）

時間

11:30〜20:00

休み

無し

料金

無料

URL

https://www.diesel.co.jp/ja/art-gallery/adam_powell

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“其中有一个特别的案例，一名囚犯选择和家人一起吃自动售货机里的食物，”沃伦回忆起那些在她的记忆中尤为深刻的盘子时说道。“还有另一个案例，他的母亲被允许进来为他烹制最后一餐。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "其中一些盘子还强调了这样一个事实：国家甚至会在死囚对发生的事情浑然不觉的情况下将其处决；其中一个盘子显示，一名囚犯选择把最后一餐留到以后吃，却不知道自己再也没有机会进食了。“其中一个盘子详细记录了一名智商为61的人被处决，”沃伦说，这表明某人在存在严重精神障碍的情况下依然被剥夺了生命。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "死囚的遭遇在艺术家兼作家加里·泰勒（Gary Tyler）的人生中占据了显要位置。1974年，泰勒年仅16岁时，被指控谋杀了一名白人少年。当他被一个全白人陪审团定罪并判处死刑时，他成为了美国最年轻的死囚。该案充斥着警方的不当行为，目前泰勒普遍被认为遭到了冤狱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1b071f0a91607e5d1e1ad3c9240e3a404aa7e9b8/38_0_1125_900/master/1125.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "绗缝面料上绣着张开的手托着蝴蝶的图案", "caption": "加里·泰勒，《费尔南达的触碰》（Gary Tyler, Fernanda’s Touch），2025年。绗缝面料、线和填充物。64英寸 x 68.25英寸。摄影：艺术家与大急流城艺术博物馆惠赠", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尽管泰勒从未获得正式平反，但在2012年“米勒诉阿拉巴马州案”（Miller v Alabama）最高法院作出裁决——即裁定对未成年被告强制判处终身监禁违宪——之后，他于2016年重获自由。", "links": [{"text": "unconstitutional", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/law/2014/jun/24/minors-life-sentences-despite-us-supreme-court-ban"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在声名狼藉的安哥拉州立监狱（Angola state prison）度过了40年——该监狱被称为南方的恶魔岛，目前是美国最大的最高安全级别监狱——泰勒开始制作被子，以安慰在监狱临终关怀病房中垂死的囚犯。起初，他很不情愿与纺织品打交道，但很快他便看到了自己的创作是多么受人珍视。“我看到自己可以帮助临终关怀病房的男人们，所以我开始对这件事产生了好感，”泰勒说。“我意识到我们正在做一件能在他们的家族中代代相传的事情。当我们的病人去世后，被子会被交到他们的家人手中，这对我来说非常感人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/785d39dac35e6c3e893d2b4192fe3b01459f9624/167_0_1666_1333/master/1666.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "使用缝纫机的男子", "caption": "加里·泰勒在工作室中。摄影：多利安·希尔（Dorian Hill），经艺术家与图书馆街集体画廊（Library Street Collective）惠赠", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着泰勒不断为垂死的囚犯制作被子，他形成了一种视角，这种视角后来塑造了他向纺织艺术创作的转变，并帮助他通过作为艺术家多年制作的复杂被子来讲述自己的故事。“你意识到那可能就是你，而且最终也会是你，你和你所照顾的人一样具有人性，”他说。“做医院志愿者是我一生中最棒的事情之一。我以前从没想过自己身上竟然有创造力的基因。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泰勒的被子通常以静态色彩为背景，其中穿插着丰富的质感和重复的图案——一种是花朵，另一种是抽象的泪滴形状。它们所描绘的场景生动而有力：一头公牛掀翻一张红色的桌子，一个男人在世界的重压下痛苦挣扎，一个戴着脚镣的孩子背对著我们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "泰勒心中最深的一个场景描绘了审判时的一个瞬间：当时他正戴着手铐、在警察的押解下离开法院，而周围的支持者则在一旁为他欢呼。“我当时涌起一股能量，”他说，“我想把双手握成拳头举起来，但我戴着手铐，副警长们抓着我的胳膊，但我还是设法展现出了一种反抗的姿态——无论发生什么，我都会继续战斗。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大急流城展览的三人组合还包括对民间刺绣艺术家雷·马特森（Ray Materson）的全面美术馆回顾展。因毒品成瘾而在监狱服刑7年期间，他出于实际需要，摸索出了用拆解的袜子进行创作的标志性技法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/0c6b5320fbf039a46f67fec27bb93869786f016a/16_0_614_767/master/614.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "中世纪场景刺绣", "caption": "雷·马特森。《贵族与女士》（Lords and Ladies），1989年。袜线。2.75in x 2in。摄影：由鲍勃·雷尼（Bob Rennie）提供", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然平角短裤和床单可以为马特森提供大量白线，但袜子对他而言有着特殊的重要性，因为它们能提供创作复杂场景所需的色彩。他会花费大量时间仅仅用来获取这些急需的材料。“雷曾对我说过一次：‘你在监狱里最大的敌人就是时钟，’”沃伦说，“对能在这项冥想般的行动中度过一天又一天的他来说，这真是一种拯救般的举动。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", article_text:
W ith nearly 2 million people behind bars, America is the global leader in incarceration. When you look at it per capita, we have the highest rate of incarceration of any independent democracy and rank fourth overall in the world, just behind El Salvador, Cuba and Turkmenistan.

Despite these troubling numbers, mass imprisonment is largely invisible. “Our carceral system is something we as a society try to separate out from the everyday,” observes Terra Warren, an associate curator at Grand Rapids Art Museum, Michigan , who alongside curator Jennifer Wcisel brings audiences three solo shows from artists Julie Green, Gary Tyler and Ray Materson. They collectively aim to make us examine more closely just what prisons are doing to our society – and how art can prove transformative to those incarcerated.

In a major feat, Green’s show collects the artist’s work The Last Supper, rarely exhibited in full. This masterpiece took 22 years to complete and comprises nearly 1,000 plates, each depicting the final meal requested by an individual on death row before their execution. Poignantly, many of the plates are simply inscribed with the word “none”, indicating when an inmate opted not to eat a final meal. One imagines it would be hard to find an appetite under such conditions.

In centering breaking bread, a practice that’s a cornerstone of our shared humanity, The Last Supper forces audiences to reckon with the contradictions of a system that at once gives the pleasure of consuming a fine meal, yet also dehumanizes and even puts to death those within its grasp. Additionally, the piece opens space for compassion and understanding by giving us a window into the lives of those who are rarely represented in any meaningful way at all.

“There’s one in particular where a prisoner opted to eat vending machine food with their family,” Warren says, recalling plates that particularly stood put in her memory. “There’s another whose mother was allowed to come in and cook their last meal.”

Some of the plates also underscore the fact that the state will put to death individuals who are not even aware of what’s happening; one plate indicates that an inmate chose to save some of their last meal for later, not understanding that there would not be a chance to ever eat again. “One of the plates details that a person with an IQ of 61 was executed,” said Warren, indicating someone was put to death in spite of serious mental impairments.

D eath row figures prominently in the life of Gary Tyler, an author and artist, who in 1974 was charged with the murder of a white teenager when Tyler was 16 years old. When he was convicted by an all-white jury and sentenced to death, he became the youngest person on death row in the United States. The case was marred by police misconduct, and Tyler is now widely considered to have been wrongfully imprisoned.

Although Tyler was never formally exonerated, he was freed in 2016 following the supreme court ruling in the 2012 Miller v Alabama case, where the court held that it was unconstitutional to adjudicate mandatory sentences of life imprisonment for juvenile defendants.

While serving four decades in the infamous Angola state prison – known as the Alcatraz of the south and currently the largest maximum-security prison in the United States – Tyler began to make quilts to comfort inmates dying in the prison’s hospice. At first reluctant to work with textiles, he soon saw just how valued his creations were. “I saw that I could help the men in the hospice, so it was something that I warmed up to,” Tyler said. “I realized we were doing something that would last for generations in the family. When our patients passed, the quilt was passed into their family, and it was really moving for me.”

As Tyler continued making quilts for dying inmates, he developed a perspective that would later inform his transition to making textile art, and that would help him be able to tell his own story through the intricate quilts that he had made for years as an artist. “You realize that that could be you, and it will be you eventually, you’re just as human as the individual you’re taking care of,” he says. “Being a hospital volunteer was one of the greatest things in my life. I never would have thought that I had the creative gene in me.”

Tyler’s quilts tend to be backgrounded by static colors shot through with rich texture and repeating motifs – flowers in one, abstract tear shapes in another. The scenes they depict are vivid and powerful: a bull smacking over a red table, a man literally struggling under the weight of the world, a child in shackles with their back turned to us.

One work that stands out in Tyler’s mind depicts a moment from the trial, when he was being led away from the courthouse in handcuffs by an escort of police, while a crowd of supporters cheered for him. “I got this surge of energy,” he says. “I wanted to raise my hands in a fist, but I had handcuffs on, with deputies holding my arms, but I still managed to show defiance, that despite what happened I would continue to fight.”

T he Grand Rapids trio is rounded out by a comprehensive museum survey of Ray Materson, the outsider embroidery artist, who developed his signature technique of working with unraveled socks by necessity while serving seven years in prison due to drug addiction.

While boxer shorts and bedsheets could supply Materson with plenty of white thread, socks were of special importance to him, as they gave him the colors that he required in order to create intricate scenes. He would spend hours and hours simply getting the dearly needed materials. “Ray said to me one time: ‘Your biggest enemy in prison is the clock,’” said Warren. “For him to be able to spend days and days in this meditative act was such a saving gesture.”

Materson’s skills quickly became known to the other inmates, who soon began asking him to make embroidery of loved ones or items such as national flags with great symbolic meaning. These pieces gave Materson a purpose and allowed the men he created for to experience a sense of identity and selfhood in a profoundly dehumanizing environment.

Life in prison has stuck with Materson, who to this day sources vintage socks like the ones he used while in jail in the 1980s. “Their nylon has the stretchability that he needs in order to work,” explained Warren. His work tends to depict intense scenes, often derived from the likes of Shakespeare, Ibsen and Chekhov, as well as royalty like Queen Victoria and Catherine the Great. While small, often measuring just 2in x 3in, the works are filled with pathos and are a wonder to behold.

“This show brings a lot of shock at the facts of what’s the reality for a lot of people, but they also bring a lot of hope,” said Warren, sharing her hopes that the art on display can both humanize and inspire, as well as show audiences that artistic creation can be transformative for them too. “Ray was on a track of death through his addiction, but because of art his life turned around into something defined by creativity and giving.”

Julie Green: The Last Supper; Gary Tyler: Rebirth and Ray Materson: Metamorphosis are all at Grand Rapids Art Museum from 3 October 2026 until 24 October 2027 (Green) and 3 January 2027 (Tyler, Materson)

editorial_title_zh: 【预览】“于垩乌帽子与战后先锋派的变身寓言集”将于10月31日起在练马区立美术馆举行：以“变身”为关键词，虚拟画家与战后前卫艺术交错的备受瞩目的展览
editorial_excerpt_zh: 练马区立美术馆（东京都练马区）将于10月31日起举办“于垩乌帽子与战后前卫派的变身寓言集”。本展以当代艺术家于垩乌帽子（1983-）为核心，汇集了战后日本致力于先锋艺术的

"paragraph", "text": "练马区立美术馆（东京都练马区）将于10月31日起举办“于垩乌帽子与战后前卫派的变身寓言集”。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本展以当代艺术家于垩乌帽子（1983-）为核心，并以“变身”为关键词，全面展出战后日本致力于先锋艺术的池田龙雄（1928-2020）、高山良策（1917-1982）、中村宏（1932-2026）等人的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
練馬区立美術館（東京都練馬区）で、「ユアサエボシと戦後アヴァンギャルドの変身寓話集」が10月31日から開催されます。

本展では、現代美術家のユアサエボシ（1983-）を軸に、戦後の日本でアヴァンギャルド芸術をこころざした池田龍雄（1928-2020）、高山良策（1917-1982）、中村宏（1932-2026）らの作品を「変身」をキーワードとして展観されます。

ユアサエボシは、古い雑誌や新聞、インターネットをもちいて集めたイメージを組み合わせ、絵画を制作しています。さらに、ユアサは絵画とともに「大正生まれの架空の三流画家 ユアサヱボシ」（1924-1987）の生涯の物語を創作して発表してきました。過去のイメージに着想を得て描くことで、架空の物故画家「ヱボシ」へと変身することから自身を「擬態派」と呼び、「ヱボシ」が生きたという戦後と現代を往還することを試みています。本展覧会でユアサは新作を発表します。それにあわせて「ヱボシ」の年譜に新たな出来事が書き加えられ、作品にまつわる新たな物語が明らかになります。

第二次世界大戦後、アヴァンギャルドの作家たちは、傷ついてゆがめられた人間やキメラ的な怪物、不気味な仮面などのイメージをとおして、戦争の記憶や戦後社会の矛盾、人間像の変容を描き出しました。これらの表現は、シュルレアリスムやルポルタージュ絵画運動に関心を寄せた作家たちの現実への深い洞察から生み出されています。彼・彼女らは見慣れた姿からの変身や変形を描くことによって、その背景にある出来事を寓話的に伝える独自の表現世界を切りひらきました。

本展では、さらに芥川（間所）紗織（1924-1966）、桂ゆき（1913-1991）、鶴岡政男（1907-1979）、古沢岩美（1912-2000）らもあわせて紹介されます。戦後美術における「変身」のモチーフの広がりをたどることは、イメージを通じた過去との対話のあらたな機会となるでしょう。

ユアサエボシと戦後アヴァンギャルドの変身寓話集

会場：練馬区立美術館（東京都練馬区貫井1-36-16）

会期：2026年10月31日（土）～12月27日（日）

開館時間：10:00～18:00 ※入館は17:30まで

休館日：月曜日（ただし、11/23［月・祝］開館。11/24［火］は休館）

観覧料：一般1,000円、高校・大学生および65～74歳800円 ※中学生以下および75歳以上無料 ※一般以外の方（無料、割引対象者）は年齢等の確認できるものを受付にて要提示 ※障害者手帳をご提示の方（介添者1名まで）は、一般500円、高校・大学生400円

アクセス：西武池袋線（東京メトロ有楽町線・副都心線直通）「中村橋」駅下車徒歩3分

詳細は、 練馬区立美術館公式サイト まで。

展示構成

第一部 戦後アヴァンギャルド

第一部では、練馬区立美術館の収蔵作家より、池田龍雄、高山良策、中村宏が取り上げられます。特攻隊としての訓練を続けるなかで終戦を迎えた池田は、戦後、上京してさまざまなジャンルの芸術家と交流しながら前衛運動にかかわりました。そのなかで、繊細で濃密なドローイングによるペン画を多数描き、政治や社会に翻弄されて変質する人間の生き方を問いました。高山は、福沢一郎絵画研究所で短期間学んだのち中国に出征し、戦後は都市や機械的な造形と民俗的でエロティックなモチーフを複雑に組み合わせた心象風景を描きました。中村は、幼少期に身近に接したセーラー服の女学生の姿と、戦時下に憧れと恐怖を抱いた飛行機や蒸気機関車とを融合させたイメージを、絵画やグラフィックの仕事において繰り返し描きました。

第二部 ユアサエボシ

第二部ではユアサエボシに焦点が当てられます。絵画制作のプロセスのなかで事後的に過去や歴史とのつながりを見出し、架空の人物「ユアサエボシ」とその生涯の物語と結びつけていく、ユアサの制作方法は、作品の多義性やあり得たかもしれない過去への想像力を喚起させるものです。現代を生きるユアサエボシは、「ヱボシ」の設定を用いることで、戦後美術を担った作家たちと疑似的に同時代を生き、制作することを試みます。

変身広場

戦争で傷ついた人間身体や、複数の生き物が混合させられた怪しい動物、あるいは、荒々しい造形の仮面などの異形の存在に変身するための道具など、「変身」にまつわるイメージは戦後美術において多様に展開されました。美術家たちは、戦中から戦後への価値観や人間像の変化や、新しい社会を求めるなかでの混乱や矛盾などを、そこに身を置きながら観察し、描き出していきました。ここでは、第一部で紹介した美術家や架空の画家「ユアサヱボシ」に、彼らと近しい場所で前衛的な表現を模索した美術家を加え、戦後美術における「変身」のモチーフのより大きな広がりが紹介されます。

激動の戦後社会を生き抜くなかで、現実の矛盾や葛藤を「変身」や「変形」という特異な造形へと昇華させたアヴァンギャルドの画家たち。本展は、池田龍雄、高山良策、中村宏らによる練馬区立美術館が誇る充実のコレクションや初公開資料を通じて激動の表現世界を振り返るとともに、大正生まれの架空の画家に「擬態」する現代美術家・ユアサエボシの新作や、直木賞作家・小川哲との刺激的なコラボレーションをも体感できる極めて意欲的な展覧会です。彼らが切りひらいた異形の寓話群は、混迷を深める現代を生きる私たちの目にも鮮烈な問いを投げかけてくることでしょう。時代を超えて交錯するイマジネーションの現場へ、ぜひ足を運んでみてはいかがでしょうか。（美術展ナビ）

"text": "第二场对谈“拉丁美洲策展的转向：拉丁美洲的张力与独立实践”将由安娜·萨拉查·埃雷拉（Ana Salazar Herrera）和阿莱西亚·塔拉（Alexia Tala）主持。该圆桌会议将反思集体记忆构建过程中的博物馆、档案和收藏等概念，探索理解、解释和激活遗产的新方式，质疑官方叙事，并让被忽视的历史和经验重焕可见性。", "translated": true}, {"type":
